body.text: Jess Wilson to become 51st Victorian premier as Coalition swept to state election victory
In short:
Liberal leader Jess Wilson will become the next premier of Victoria after the Coalition defeated Labor in the state election.
The Coalition was last elected to government in Victoria in 2010, holding power for one single four-year term.
Ms Wilson has campaigned strongly on potholes, crime and the state's debt while also announcing cuts and privatisation plans just days ahead of election day.
Liberal leader Jess Wilson will become Victoria's first popularly elected female premier as the Coalition dislodges Labor from state government after 12 years.
Ahead of Ms Wilson's acceptance speech at Liberal headquarters in Melbourne, party faithful chanted: "Jess we can."
After taking to the stage, Ms Wilson declared a "mandate to start to bring hope back to Victoria".
"Tonight I declare that Victoria is back open for business.
Victorians had "drawn a line in the sand after 12 long years", she said.
"Victorians have sent a clear message that they cannot allow the state to continue on the direction it has been going in under Labor," Ms Wilson said.
She said Labor's biggest failure was "that they stopped trusting the Victorian people with the truth".
"Victorians have put their trust in me tonight, and I will always return that trust with the truth. That's my commitment, that's the kind of premier I want to be," she said.
Conceding she had a big job ahead of her, Ms Wilson said the work starts tomorrow.
"We can't fix Victoria overnight. It will take many years of hard work and responsible governing to get Victoria back to the place it used to be," Ms Wilson said.
Federal deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume said Ms Wilson was an "extraordinary leader" and has been able to galvanise and unite Coalition with new energy.
"Jess Wilson, her slogan was 'make a fresh start'. And it actually was," she said.
"That's exactly what people were looking for."
Labor leader congratulates next premier
Labor leader Ben Carroll, who lost his own seat of Niddrie, called Ms Wilson to concede defeat before 8:30pm on election night.
Addressing the Labor faithful, Mr Carroll congratulated and sent his "best wishes" to Ms Wilson.
"She's achieved a great thing as Victoria's youngest and first elected female premier,"
Mr Carroll said the results showed Victorians were sending a clear message that they wanted change.
"I will always love our great state no matter who runs it," he said.

While reeling off a number of Labor's achievements over the last 12 years, he made a dig at a late promise by the Liberal Party, claiming Labor was able to lower debt and see a budget surplus without privatising water assets.

Just two days before polling day, while announcing the Coalition's costings, Ms Wilson announced plans to partly privatise Melbourne's sewerage network, cut and delay level crossing removals and walk back Labor plans to expand free kindergarten.
Those announcements drew sharp criticism from Labor, One Nation and the Greens, especially given 2.2 million Victorians had already cast their ballots in early voting by that time.
Mr Carroll said the party would spend the next four years winning Victorians over and regaining the trust of people who did not vote for them.
"This is a significant loss for Labor. It's not the result we wanted, but it is a result we accept," Mr Carroll said.
"As leader, I take full responsibility," he said.
"There will be a lot of talking after this result but right now Labor needs to listen, and we need to listen as a united team, not a divided one."
'Simply devastating' result for Victorian Labor
It has been a swift rise for the 36-year-old who became the first woman to lead the Victorian Liberal Party after ousting Brad Battin in November 2025.
It was the party's fifth leadership change in seven years, with Ms Wilson's ascension marking the end of a tumultuous period for the Victorian Liberals.
In less than four years, Ms Wilson has gone from making her maiden speech in state parliament as the new member for Kew to premier of Victoria.
Ahead of the election, Ms Wilson ran a strong social media campaign on potholes, crime and the state's debt, with minimal slip-ups.
Labor's popularity had plummeted after more than a decade in government.

When he took power from Jacinta Allan in July, Mr Carroll called a royal commission into allegations of crime and corruption on major infrastructure projects and distanced himself from Ms Allan and the premier before her, Daniel Andrews.
But he inherited the baggage of a Labor government, which he had served as a senior minister, associated with questionable integrity, increased crime and soaring state debt.
Speaking to the ABC tonight, deputy Labor leader Gabrielle Williams said there was "deep community anger" over allegations of union corruption in the construction sector.
Ms Williams said the result was "simply devastating" for Labor and that she wanted to "stick around" and help the party rebuild.
Redbridge pollster and former Labor strategist Kos Samaras said Labor had lost seats in Victoria that the party had held since the federation of Australia.
"This is just the most historic event the Labor Party has experienced nationally,"
he said.
Mr Samaras said it could take a decade or more for Labor to recover in Victoria and would require soul-searching for "the full extent of next year".
"I think the next Labor premier is probably still in high school," he said.
